chapters.title: Foundations
chapters.intro: Knife work, heat, seasoning and the mise en place that every French kitchen stands on. Learn these first, and every chapter after reads as a variation on them.

chapters.title: The mother sauces
chapters.intro: Béchamel, velouté, espagnole, tomato and hollandaise, and the small sauces each one gives. Learn the liaison and the liquid of each mother, and the family tree follows.

chapters.title: Butter and emulsions
chapters.intro: How butter, yolk, acid and water are coaxed into one smooth sauce, and why they part again. From beurre blanc to mayonnaise, the same physics holds every one of them together.

chapters.title: Methods
chapters.intro: Braising, poaching, sautéing, roasting and the other ways heat meets food in the classical kitchen. Each method is a set of choices about fat, liquid and temperature, made for a reason.

chapters.title: Creole and Cajun
chapters.intro: The roux, the trinity and the great pots of south Louisiana, and where the city's Creole cooking parts from the Cajun cooking of the country. Gumbo, étouffée and jambalaya are the lessons.

chapters.title: The larder
chapters.intro: Stocks, charcuterie, cold preparations and the ingredients a classical kitchen keeps to hand. Good buying and good keeping decide the plate long before any cooking begins.

chapters.title: The old houses
chapters.intro: Antoine's, Galatoire's, Arnaud's, Commander's Palace and the other dining rooms that made New Orleans a restaurant city. Each house kept dishes that the rest of the country later learned from.

chapters.title: Brennan's
chapters.intro: The house on Royal Street, its breakfast, its sauces and the dishes it made famous. Every entry ties a classical idea to a plate you will carry to the table.

chapters.title: Pastry
chapters.intro: Doughs, creams, custards and the sugar work behind the dessert menu. Precision matters most here, so ratios and temperatures lead every entry in the chapter.

chapters.title: Kitchen French
chapters.intro: The words a brigade uses at the pass, from mise en place to à la minute. Say them well and the kitchen hears that you know the work behind them.

chapters.title: History
chapters.intro: From Carême and Escoffier to the Creole cookbooks of nineteenth century New Orleans, the people and books that shaped this cooking. The dates and the sources travel with every claim.

chapters.title: Food safety
chapters.intro: Temperatures, times and the habits that keep a kitchen's food fit to serve. Every figure in this chapter is taken from its source, and the source is shown beside it.

entries.title: Mise en place
entries.summary: Mise en place, everything in its place, is the work a cook does before the first ticket: ingredients prepared, tools set out and a plan in the head, so that service is spent cooking rather than searching.

entries.title: Knife cuts
entries.summary: The classical knife cuts give every vegetable a named shape and size, from the tiny brunoise to the large dice, so that pieces cook evenly, look clean on the plate and yield the same every time.

entries.title: Heat and the pan
entries.say: As it reads: heat and the pan.
entries.summary: How heat travels into food, why browning needs a hot, dry surface, how the stove's heat ladder and each kind of pan behave, and how a cook reads heat with the ear, the eye, the nose and the probe.

entries.title: White stock
entries.say: As it reads: white stock, or fond blanc, fohn BLAHN.
entries.summary: Fond blanc, white stock, is chicken or veal bones simmered gently from cold water with a pale mirepoix and herbs, never roasted, for a clear, light, gelatinous liquid that becomes velouté, suprême, allemande and the white soups.

entries.title: Brown stock
entries.say: As it reads: brown stock, or fond brun, fohn BRUHN.
entries.summary: Veal or beef bones roasted deep brown with onion, carrot, celery and tomato purée, then simmered for hours in cold water, unsalted. Full of gelatine, it is the base of espagnole, demi-glace, glace de viande and every classical brown sauce.

entries.title: Fumet de poisson
entries.summary: A quick stock of lean white fish bones sweated in butter with aromatics, wetted with white wine and cold water and simmered for only 20 to 30 minutes. It is the base of fish velouté, the white wine sauces and the poaching liquor for fish.

entries.title: Court-bouillon and nage
entries.summary: A court-bouillon is a short broth of water, an acid, aromatics and salt, simmered briefly to flavour and poach fish and seafood. Refined, reduced and mounted with butter, it becomes a nage, a broth fine enough to serve.

entries.title: Glace de viande and the glaces
entries.summary: A glace is stock reduced slowly until syrupy, setting firm when cold: glace de viande from brown stock, glace de volaille from chicken, glace de poisson from fish. A spoonful deepens a sauce; it is the concentrated end of the stockpot.

entries.title: Roux
entries.summary: Flour cooked in fat in equal weights, then whisked into a liquid and simmered to thicken it. The classical binder of French sauces: cooked white for béchamel, blond for velouté and brown for espagnole, and taken far darker in Louisiana.

entries.title: Beurre manié, slurries and liaisons
entries.say: As it reads: slurries and liaisons, with beurre manié, burr mahn-YAY.
entries.summary: The thickeners beyond roux: beurre manié kneaded from butter and flour, starch slurries of cornflour or arrowroot, the egg yolk and cream liaison, reduction, and the old binders. Each is chosen for flavour, clarity, holding time and what the guest can eat.

entries.title: Clarifying: the consommé raft
entries.say: As it reads: clarifying, and consommé, kohn-so-MAY.
entries.summary: Consommé is a rich stock cleared to crystal brightness by a raft of minced lean meat, egg whites, mirepoix and tomato, which rises, sets and filters the stock as it barely simmers: the patient cook's test, and the clear soup of the old menus.

entries.title: Seasoning and tasting
entries.say: As it reads: seasoning and tasting.
entries.summary: Seasoning is the cook's constant job: salt, acid, pepper and heat added and adjusted by tasting, with a clean spoon every time. Salt early in a braise and late in a reduction, and taste the plate as a whole.

entries.title: The idea of the mother sauces
entries.summary: A mother sauce is a base that many smaller sauces grow from. Carême named four, Escoffier's Guide of 1903 named four of its own, and later schools taught five. Learn the liquid and the thickener of each, and the family follows.

entries.title: Béchamel
entries.summary: Béchamel is milk thickened with a white roux and seasoned with salt, white pepper and nutmeg. It is the gentlest mother sauce and the first one a cook learns, the base of gratins, croquettes and soufflés.

entries.title: Velouté
entries.summary: Velouté is white stock, veal, chicken or fish, thickened with a blond roux and simmered until glossy. The name means velvety. It is a working base, seldom served plain, and the root of the pale stock sauces.

entries.title: Espagnole
entries.summary: Espagnole is brown stock thickened with a brown roux, built with browned mirepoix, tomato and often bacon, then simmered for hours and skimmed. Rarely served alone, it is the parent of demi-glace and so of the whole brown family.

entries.title: Sauce tomate
entries.summary: The classical French tomato sauce: tomatoes cooked with salt pork, a mirepoix, garlic and white stock, then passed through a sieve until smooth. One of Escoffier's four base sauces, it is the parent of provençale and portugaise, and New Orleans' Creole sauce is its cousin.

entries.title: Hollandaise
entries.summary: A warm emulsion of egg yolk and butter, sharpened with lemon juice or a vinegar reduction. It is the one mother sauce bound by egg yolk: quick to make, fragile in service and the parent of a whole family.

entries.title: Béarnaise
entries.summary: Hollandaise built on a sharp reduction of white wine, tarragon vinegar, shallot and tarragon, and finished with fresh herbs. Firmer and sharper than its parent, it is the classic sauce for grilled beef and the base of Choron and Foyot.

entries.title: Marchand de vin
entries.summary: The wine merchant's sauce: red wine and shallot reduced into a brown sauce. New Orleans made its own glossy version of onion, garlic, often ham and mushroom, red wine and beef stock, and Brennan's serves it beneath the egg on the Eggs Hussarde.

entries.title: Choron and Foyot
entries.summary: Two daughters of béarnaise, each made by one addition. Choron folds in tomato cooked down to a thick paste, coral and tangy; Foyot whisks in glace de viande, a reduced meat glaze, tawny and deeper. Brennan's serves both.

entries.title: Demi-glace
entries.summary: Espagnole and brown stock simmered together and reduced by half until glossy: the working mother of the classical brown sauces. Bordelaise, Robert, chasseur, madère and périgueux start from it, and many modern kitchens make it from reduced brown stock alone.

entries.title: Bordelaise, French and New Orleans
entries.summary: Two sauces share the name. French bordelaise is red wine, shallot and herbs reduced into demi-glace and finished with beef marrow; New Orleans bordelaise is a garlic butter with parsley. Knowing which is on the plate changes the wine and the promise.

entries.title: The béchamel family
entries.summary: The small sauces built on béchamel: Mornay with cheese, Soubise with onion, Nantua with crayfish, crème with cream and cardinal with lobster butter. Each is béchamel plus one defining addition, and the cousins run from macaroni cheese to Oysters Bienville.

entries.title: The velouté family
entries.summary: The daughters of velouté: suprême and allemande on the chicken and veal side, vin blanc, Bercy and normande on the fish side, and a run of small sauces each made by one addition. Learn the stock, then the finish.

entries.title: The brown family
entries.say: As it reads: the brown family.
entries.summary: The small sauces built on demi-glace: Robert, charcutière, chasseur, diable, piquante, lyonnaise, poivrade, bigarade and the game sauces. Each follows one pattern: an aromatic, an acid reduction, the brown base and a finish.

entries.title: Madère, Périgueux and the wine-finished sauces
entries.summary: Brown sauces finished with fortified wine: madère, Périgueux and périgourdine with truffle, financière, and the Madeira, port and sherry that finish sauces and soups. The rule: add the wine late and never boil it hard.

entries.title: The hollandaise and béarnaise families
entries.summary: The daughters of hollandaise and béarnaise: mousseline, maltaise, Mikado, noisette and moutarde on one side, Paloise, Choron and Foyot on the other. Each is acid, yolks and butter with one defining addition.

entries.title: Reading the sauce tree
entries.say: As it reads: reading the sauce tree.
entries.summary: Every classical sauce is a mother, a defining addition and a finish. Learn to read a sauce's name as directions, to a place, a person or a garnish, and any French sauce on any menu becomes something you can explain.

entries.title: Finishing a sauce
entries.say: As it reads: finishing a sauce.
entries.summary: Everything a cook does between a sauce that is cooked and a sauce that is ready: reducing it to nappe, skimming, passing it through a fine sieve, protecting its surface, holding it at the right heat and tasting it last.

entries.title: The sauces in Le Guide culinaire
entries.summary: How Escoffier ordered the sauce chapter of Le Guide culinaire (1903): four great base sauces with their working bases, then the small sauces, English sauces, cold sauces and compound butters, and how to read the old text today.

entries.title: Beurre blanc
entries.summary: White butter: a sharp reduction of white wine, vinegar and shallot with cold butter whisked in piece by piece over low heat. No egg yolks hold it, only the butter itself, so it lives in a narrow warm window.

entries.title: Beurre monté
entries.summary: Butter whisked piece by piece into a little boiling water until it becomes a creamy, pourable liquid. Neutral, with no acid and no reduction, it is a cooking medium for poaching lobster and fish, glazing vegetables and keeping food moist.

entries.title: Beurre noisette and beurre noir
entries.summary: Brown butter: butter cooked until its milk solids toast to the colour of hazelnuts and it smells nutty, then stopped at once. Taken darker and sharpened with vinegar and capers, it is beurre noir. Seconds separate brown from burnt.

entries.title: À la meunière
entries.summary: The miller's wife's way with fish: seasoned, dusted in flour and sautéed golden in clarified butter, then dressed at the last moment with foaming brown butter, lemon juice and parsley. New Orleans kitchens make a richer brown sauce of their own.

entries.title: Amandine
entries.summary: Amandine is fish cooked the meunière way and finished with flaked almonds toasted golden in brown butter, with lemon and parsley. It is the method behind New Orleans's trout amandine, and the template for the Louisiana habit of putting pecans in the pan.

entries.title: Clarified butter
entries.summary: Clarified butter is butter with its water and milk solids taken away, leaving pure golden butterfat. It takes more heat than whole butter without burning, gives a firmer hollandaise and is the cooking fat of a meunière.

entries.title: Compound butters
entries.summary: Compound butters, beurres composés in French, are softened butter worked with a flavouring, rolled, chilled and sliced. A disc melts over hot grilled meat or fish into an instant sauce; others, such as crustacean butter, finish classic sauces.

entries.title: Mayonnaise
entries.summary: Mayonnaise is a cold emulsion of egg yolk and oil, seasoned with mustard and sharpened with vinegar or lemon. It is the cold cousin of hollandaise and the parent of rémoulade, tartare, verte and a family of cold sauces.

entries.title: Aïoli and the French rémoulade
entries.summary: Aïoli is the garlic sauce of Provence: garlic pounded with salt, olive oil worked in, usually with a yolk. The French rémoulade is mayonnaise with mustard, gherkins, capers, herbs and anchovy. Rouille, tartare and gribiche complete the family.

entries.title: Vinaigrette
entries.summary: Vinaigrette is oil and vinegar whisked into a temporary emulsion, classically three parts oil to one of acid, with salt, mustard and shallot dissolved in the acid first. Warm versions of bacon fat or brown butter coat leaves better.

entries.title: Mignonette
entries.say: min-yo-NET (meen-yo-NET, nearer the French, is also heard)
entries.summary: Mignonette is the raw oyster’s sauce: finely chopped shallot in red wine or Champagne vinegar with coarsely cracked black pepper. A spoonful lifts the oyster’s brine without drowning it; ours adds preserved Fresno chilli and parsley.

entries.title: How emulsions hold, break and come back
entries.say: As it reads: how emulsions hold, break and come back.
entries.summary: An emulsion is fat held in tiny droplets through water, or water through fat, by an emulsifier such as yolk, butter’s milk proteins or mustard. Heat, cold and haste break it; warm water, a fresh yolk or cold butter usually brings it back.

entries.title: Sauté and the shallow fry
entries.summary: Sautéing cooks small or thin pieces fast in a little hot fat, tossed or turned; shallow frying uses more fat and a coating. Heat, a dry surface and room in the pan decide whether food browns or steams.

entries.title: Pan-roast and poêlé
entries.summary: Two ways to roast in a pan. Pan-roasting sears on the stove, finishes in a hot oven and bastes with butter on its return; poêlé roasts tender meat in butter on vegetables in a covered pot, uncovered at the end to colour.

entries.title: Braise and daube
entries.summary: Braising sears a tough, hard-working cut, then cooks it slowly, covered, with wine or stock partway up, until its collagen melts into gelatine and the liquid becomes its sauce. A daube is Provence’s red wine braise, marinated first.

entries.title: Poaching, shallow and deep
entries.summary: Poaching cooks food gently in liquid held below the simmer, so eggs, fish and chicken stay moist and nothing browns. Deep poaching submerges the food; shallow poaching half covers fish on shallots and turns the liquor into the sauce.

entries.title: Eggs to order and the omelette
entries.say: As it reads: eggs to order and the omelette.
entries.summary: Fried, scrambled, boiled and rolled: the everyday eggs of a breakfast kitchen, each a matter of heat, fat and timing. The cook makes exactly what the ticket asks, and the French omelette is the test every cook is set.

entries.title: Boil, blanch and steam
entries.say: As it reads: boil, blanch and steam.
entries.summary: Three water methods every cook uses daily: a rolling boil in salted water for pasta and green vegetables, a brief blanch and an iced refresh to set colour and prepare for service, and steam for gentle, moist cooking that keeps shape.

entries.title: En papillote
entries.summary: Food sealed in a parcel of paper, foil or leaf and baked, so it steams in its own juices with its aromatics. The parcel puffs as the steam builds, and the burst of scent when it is opened is the point.

entries.title: Confit
entries.summary: From the French confire, to preserve: meat salted, then cooked slowly submerged in fat until it is meltingly tender, and kept under that fat. Duck leg is the classic; garlic, tomato and fish are cooked the same gentle way in oil.

entries.title: Roast and baste
entries.say: As it reads: roast and baste.
entries.summary: Roasting cooks meat or poultry in the dry heat of an oven: high heat to brown the outside, lower heat to cook it through. Basting adds colour and flavour, and resting lets carryover heat finish the centre.

entries.title: Grill and salamander
entries.say: As it reads: grill and salamander.
entries.summary: Grilling cooks food on bars over heat from below, marking it and flavouring it with smoke from the dripping fat. The salamander is the professional kitchen's overhead grill (broiler): fierce heat from above for finishing, glazing and gratins.

entries.title: Smoking, hot and cold
entries.summary: Smoking flavours food with the smoke of smouldering wood. Hot smoking cooks as it flavours, as with andouille and tasso; cold smoking flavours without cooking and always follows a cure. Today smoke is mostly a seasoning.

entries.title: Frying and the fry station
entries.summary: Deep frying cooks food submerged in clean oil at about 170 to 190°C (338 to 374°F): surface water flashes to steam, the coating sets crisp, and the inside cooks gently in its own moisture.

entries.title: Deglaze and the pan sauce
entries.say: As it reads: deglaze, pan sauce.
entries.summary: A pan sauce is made in minutes in the pan a piece of meat or fish was seared in: the browned juices are lifted with wine or stock, reduced, enriched and finished, so nothing the searing made goes to waste.

entries.title: Monter au beurre
entries.summary: To mount a sauce with butter: cold butter swirled or whisked into a hot sauce, off the boil, at the last moment, for gloss, body and a rounder taste. Simple to do and easy to undo, because a sauce that reboils breaks.

entries.title: Flambé
entries.summary: Flambé means flamed: spirit added to a hot pan and lit, so its vapour burns in a short burst of flame. It burns off some alcohol, never all, adds aroma and a touch of caramel, and gives the dining room a show.

entries.title: Creole and Cajun
entries.summary: Creole cooking is the city's: New Orleans households and restaurants, French technique with butter, cream and tomato. Cajun cooking is the country's: the Acadians' descendants on the bayous and prairies, with smoked meats, dark roux and rice.

entries.title: The holy trinity and the mirepoix
entries.summary: Onion, celery and green bell pepper, diced and softened together at the start of a Creole or Cajun dish. It is south Louisiana's answer to the French mirepoix, with green pepper standing where the carrot would be.

entries.title: The roux ladder
entries.summary: The Louisiana roux ladder runs from white and blond through peanut butter and milk chocolate to dark chocolate, or brick. Each rung takes longer, tastes deeper and thickens less, and each dish wants its own rung.

entries.title: Gumbo
entries.summary: Gumbo is Louisiana's soup-stew, served over rice and thickened with roux, okra, filé or a mix of them. Its name most likely comes from a Bantu word for okra, and its pot holds the state's history.

entries.title: Roux, okra and filé
entries.summary: The three ways a Louisiana cook gives a gumbo its body: a roux of flour cooked in fat, okra cooked down until its sticky juice thickens the pot, and filé, ground sassafras leaves stirred in at the end.

entries.title: Seafood gumbo
entries.summary: A New Orleans classic: Gulf shrimp, blue crab and oysters in a dark broth built on roux, the trinity and a stock of shells, often with tomato and smoked sausage, the seafood added last and served over rice.

entries.title: Gumbo z'herbes
entries.summary: Green gumbo: an odd number of greens, collards, mustard, turnip tops, spinach and cabbage among them, cooked down and chopped or puréed. Once a meatless Lenten dish, it is now the rich Holy Thursday gumbo of New Orleans.

entries.title: Étouffée
entries.summary: Smothered: crawfish tails or shrimp in a thick, buttery sauce of blond to peanut butter roux, the trinity and a little shell stock, spooned over rice. A sauce rather than a soup, and in its crawfish form a Cajun classic.

entries.title: Jambalaya, red and brown
entries.summary: Rice cooked in one pot with meat, seafood or both, the grains drinking a seasoned stock until none is left. Red jambalaya, with tomato, belongs to the city; brown, coloured by well-browned meat and onions, belongs to the Cajun country.

entries.title: Creole courtbouillon
entries.summary: Redfish cooked gently in a thick, rust-red gravy of roux, tomato and the trinity, with garlic, bay, lemon and wine, and served over rice. Said coo-bee-YON in Louisiana, it borrows a French word and means a different dish.

entries.title: Sauce piquante
entries.summary: A Cajun stew rather than a sauce: meat, game or seafood simmered long in a dark roux gravy with the trinity, tomato and plenty of cayenne and hot pepper, served over rice. Piquante means sharp, and the heat is the point.

entries.title: Creole sauce
entries.summary: The New Orleans tomato sauce: onion, celery and green pepper softened in fat with garlic, then tomatoes, stock, bay, thyme and cayenne, simmered thick. It is the backbone of shrimp Creole and of many Creole fish and egg dishes.

entries.title: Creole rémoulade
entries.summary: The New Orleans rémoulade is a cold, spiced sauce led by Creole mustard, with paprika, cayenne, horseradish, lemon, garlic, celery, green onion and parsley. Pinker and hotter than the French one, it is the sauce of shrimp rémoulade.

entries.title: Ravigote, French and New Orleans
entries.summary: Ravigote is a sharp, herb-led sauce whose name means revived. In France it is a cold vinaigrette with capers, shallot and fines herbes, or a warm velouté sauce; in New Orleans it is lump crab in a cold, creamy dressing.

entries.title: New Orleans barbecue shrimp
entries.say: As it reads: New Orleans barbecue shrimp.
entries.summary: New Orleans barbecue shrimp are never barbecued: head-on shrimp cooked in a peppery pan sauce of butter, Worcestershire, garlic and lemon. Credited to Pascal's Manale, the dish is eaten with the hands, a bib and plenty of bread.

entries.title: Blackening
entries.summary: Blackening is Paul Prudhomme's method: a fillet dipped in melted butter, coated in a paprika-led spice blend and seared in a dry cast-iron pan heated past smoking, so the spices toast to a dark crust while the inside stays moist.

entries.title: Grillades and grits
entries.summary: Thin pieces of veal or beef round, pounded, seasoned, browned hard and braised in a brown roux gravy with the trinity and tomato until fork tender, then spooned over slow-cooked grits. A Creole brunch classic with country roots.

entries.title: Red beans and rice
entries.say: As it reads: red beans and rice.
entries.summary: Red kidney beans simmered slowly with the trinity, garlic, bay and a ham bone or pickled pork until the pot turns creamy, served with rice and sausage. New Orleans's Monday dish and a signature of the city.

entries.title: Creole tomato
entries.summary: A Louisiana-grown tomato picked ripe, not a single variety: the name comes from the river-soil farms of St. Bernard and Plaquemines parishes. Sweet, sharp and juicy, it is a summer crop, eaten raw and cooked into the city's tomato dishes.

entries.title: Gulf shrimp
entries.summary: Wild shrimp from the Gulf coast, mostly brown and white, are the backbone of New Orleans cooking. Know the species and their seasons, read the count per pound, cook them briefly and say plainly where they come from.

entries.title: Crawfish
entries.summary: Crawfish are small freshwater crustaceans, mostly red swamp crawfish, farmed in Louisiana's rice fields and trapped wild in the Atchafalaya Basin. They are boiled whole in spring, and their tail meat and golden fat carry étouffée, bisque and pies all year.

entries.title: Blue crab and lump crabmeat
entries.summary: The blue crab of the Gulf and Atlantic, Louisiana's great crab catch, reaches the kitchen as picked meat sold by grade, as claws and as soft-shells. Know the grades, pick the meat over and fold it gently so the lumps stay whole.

entries.title: Gulf oysters
entries.summary: The eastern oyster of Louisiana's brackish bays: milder and plumper where river water freshens the bay, brinier where the sea pushes in. Eaten raw, chargrilled, fried, baked and in gumbo, and on four Brennan's dishes.

entries.title: Redfish, drum and the Gulf fish
entries.say: As it reads: redfish, drum, Gulf fish.
entries.summary: Redfish, the red drum, is the Gulf's firm, mild, copper-red fish with a black spot by its tail. Learn it, its cousins and the day's catch, how round and flat fish are cut, and why redfish left commercial nets.

entries.title: Andouille
entries.summary: Cajun andouille is a coarse pork sausage, heavy with garlic and pepper and smoked for hours until dark and firm. It is made to season a pot, browned first so its fat and smoke flavour gumbo, jambalaya and red beans.

entries.title: Tasso
entries.say: TAH-so (TASS-oh is also heard; confirm the house habit)
entries.summary: Tasso is Cajun seasoning meat: strips of pork shoulder briefly cured, coated in cayenne, garlic and spice, and hot-smoked until firm. Diced small, a little seasons a whole pot of beans, gumbo or Creole sauce.

entries.title: Boudin
entries.summary: Cajun boudin is a fresh sausage of cooked pork, pork liver, rice, onion, green onion and pepper, heated in its casing and eaten hot, squeezed from the skin. It is Acadiana's everyday snack, sold by the link at meat markets and roadside counters.

entries.title: Filé
entries.summary: Filé is the ground dried leaf of the sassafras tree, a Choctaw ingredient taken up by Creole and Cajun cooks. Earthy and woody, with a hint of root beer, it seasons and thickens gumbo, and it goes in off the heat.

entries.title: Okra
entries.summary: Okra is the green seed pod of a plant in the mallow family, carried from West and Central Africa through the slave trade. Cut and simmered, it releases a slippery gel that thickens gumbo; fried or pickled, it stays crisp.

entries.title: Louisiana rice
entries.summary: Louisiana grows its rice on the south-west prairie around Crowley, and rice sits under or inside most Creole and Cajun dishes. Long grain is the everyday rice, cooked to stay separate; popcorn rice is the aromatic local long grain.

entries.title: Cane syrup and Steen's
entries.say: As it reads: cane syrup and Steen's.
entries.summary: Pure cane syrup is sugar cane juice boiled down in open kettles to a dark, glossy syrup with nothing taken out. Gentler than molasses and different from sorghum, it is Louisiana's pouring syrup, and Steen's of Abbeville has made it since 1910.

entries.title: Creole mustard
entries.summary: A coarse, spicy whole-grain mustard of brown mustard seeds steeped in vinegar, often sharpened with horseradish. New Orleans keeps it for rémoulade, sandwiches, glazes, crab cakes and dressings, and its heat is fragile: it fades with boiling.

entries.title: Louisiana hot sauces
entries.say: As it reads: Louisiana hot sauces.
entries.summary: Louisiana-style hot sauce is aged red peppers, vinegar and salt, thin enough to shake. Tabasco from Avery Island and Crystal from New Orleans are the two famous bottles, and the table uses them to season, not to burn.

entries.title: Chicory coffee
entries.summary: Roasted, ground chicory root blended with coffee: a darker, more bitter, fuller cup with less caffeine than straight coffee. A French habit New Orleans kept, poured as café au lait at the French Market and baked into Brennan's Café Brûlot Coffee Cake.

entries.title: Pecans
entries.summary: The pecan is a hickory nut native to the Mississippi valley and the South, rich, buttery and quick to toast. New Orleans cooks put it where French recipes put almonds: in pralines, pies, crusts for fish and butter sauces.

entries.title: Leidenheimer and New Orleans French bread
entries.summary: New Orleans French bread is a long loaf with a thin crust that shatters and a light, cottony crumb, softer than a Paris baguette. Leidenheimer, baking since 1896, makes the loaf most po-boys are built on.

entries.title: Mirliton, satsuma and Creole cream cheese
entries.summary: Three foods of the New Orleans household larder: the mirliton, a pale green squash stuffed for the holidays; the satsuma, a seedless Plaquemines mandarin; and Creole cream cheese, a tangy cultured cheese eaten for breakfast. Each is rarely seen on restaurant menus.

entries.title: Eggs and yolks
entries.say: As it reads: eggs and yolks.
entries.summary: The hen's egg is the kitchen's binder, leavener, emulsifier and sauce base: a white of water and protein around a yolk of fat and lecithin. Freshness, grade and size decide how it poaches, peels and holds a sauce.

entries.title: Butter
entries.summary: Cream churned until its fat gathers: about 80 per cent fat with water and milk solids, which is why butter browns, burns and splits. The kitchen clarifies it, chills it or mounts it to suit the job, and cooks with unsalted.

entries.title: Cream and crème fraîche
entries.say: As it reads: cream; creme fraiche, krem FRESH.
entries.summary: Cream is the fat skimmed from milk, sold by its fat: the more fat, the better it whips, the harder it can boil and the less it splits. Crème fraîche is cream thickened and soured by cultures, and mascarpone its richer Italian cousin.

entries.title: Mushrooms
entries.summary: The cultivated kinds a kitchen buys, button to king oyster, and the wild ones by season; a mushroom is mostly water, so it browns only in a hot, uncrowded pan with the salt held back. Dried, pickled or preserved, it keeps its savoury depth.

entries.title: Red wine in the kitchen
entries.summary: Dry red wine is a seasoning in a French kitchen: it lifts the browned bits from a pan, brings acid and tannin, and reduces into the deep sauces of the house. A sound bottle is the only kind to cook with.

entries.title: Capers
entries.summary: The unopened flower bud of a Mediterranean shrub, picked by hand and cured in salt or brine until it turns briny, sharp and faintly floral. A small bite that cuts fat, from the tartare dressing to the Grenobloise.

entries.title: Preserved lemon
entries.summary: Lemons packed in salt and their own juice for weeks until the rind turns soft, translucent and perfumed: a North African larder staple a kitchen can make itself, salty and floral rather than sour, and used for its rind.

entries.title: Beef tenderloin and the Chateaubriand
entries.say: As it reads: beef tenderloin; Chateaubriand, shah-toh-bree-AHN.
entries.summary: The tenderloin is the long, lean muscle along the inside of the backbone that does almost no work, so it is the most tender cut and the mildest. The filet mignon, the Chateaubriand and the steak tartare are all cut from it.

entries.title: Lamb and the shank
entries.summary: Lamb is the meat of a sheep under a year old, and its cuts divide by the work the muscle did. The shank, the lower leg, is the slow-cooked cut: it melts over hours into a tender braise and a glossy jus.

entries.title: Swordfish
entries.summary: A large ocean fish sold as thick steaks or fillets: firm, dense and mildly sweet, cooked more like meat than like a flaky fillet. It dries fast once the centre turns opaque, so it is seared hard, pulled early and rested.

entries.title: Tuna
entries.summary: The tunas a kitchen names by colour, fat and price: yellowfin, bigeye, albacore and bluefin. Firm and meaty, deep red to pale pink, and the fish most often served raw, so its handling and its advisory matter as much as any cooking.

entries.title: Rye and caraway
entries.say: As it reads: rye and caraway; tuile, TWEEL.
entries.summary: Rye is the dense, earthy grain of northern Europe and the deli sandwich; caraway is the warm, anise-edged seed most people take for the taste of rye bread. On the fall tartare they meet as a rye tuile and Montreal seasoning.

entries.title: Fresh pasta and agnolotti
entries.say: As it reads: fresh pasta; agnolotti del plin, ah-nyoh-LOT-tee del PLEEN.
entries.summary: Fresh egg pasta is soft wheat flour and egg rolled thin and cooked in a minute or two; dried pasta is durum semolina and water, extruded and dried to a firm bite. The menu carries both: pinched agnolotti, rough frascarelli, shells and buttered noodles.

entries.title: Dark chocolate
entries.say: As it reads: dark chocolate; cremeux, kray-MUH.
entries.summary: Chocolate is roasted cocoa bean ground to a paste, with cocoa butter and sugar added; a bar's percentage is the share that came from the bean. That share sets dark, bittersweet, milk and white, and the pastry kitchen melts, sets and tempers it.

entries.title: Oysters Rockefeller
entries.summary: Oysters on the half shell under a green sauce of puréed herbs and greens, butter and breadcrumbs, baked or glazed until bubbling. Created at Antoine's in 1889, or 1899 by some accounts, it has a secret recipe; every other kitchen makes its own version.

entries.title: Oysters Bienville
entries.summary: Baked oysters under a thick, rich sauce of shrimp, mushrooms, green onion and garlic, bound with roux and cream and enriched with yolk, finished with sherry, crumbs and cheese. Named for the founder of New Orleans, and claimed by two old houses.

entries.title: Shrimp rémoulade and Shrimp Arnaud
entries.summary: Chilled boiled Gulf shrimp dressed in a sharp Creole rémoulade on shredded lettuce, a starter of the old New Orleans houses. Shrimp Arnaud is Arnaud's own version, in its red rémoulade, and the house's signature starter.

entries.title: Trout meunière and amandine at Galatoire's
entries.say: TROWT muhn-YEHR and ah-mahn-DEEN at GAL-uh-twahrz
entries.summary: Speckled trout, the Gulf's delicate spotted sea trout, floured and fried or sautéed, then covered with a dark New Orleans brown butter meunière and toasted almonds: Galatoire's trout meunière amandine, a classic of the Bourbon Street house.

entries.title: Pompano en papillote
entries.summary: Antoine's dish of pompano baked in a sealed paper parcel over a sauce of shrimp and crabmeat in a white wine velouté. The parcel puffs with steam in the oven and is cut open at the table.

entries.title: Creole turtle soup
entries.say: As it reads: Creole turtle soup.
entries.summary: New Orleans' dark, thick turtle soup: turtle meat simmered with a brown roux, the trinity, tomato, stock and Worcestershire, finished with sherry, lemon and chopped hard-boiled egg. A Creole answer to the clear turtle soups of old banquets.

entries.title: Café brûlot
entries.summary: Burnt coffee: brandy and orange liqueur flamed in a bowl with sugar, cinnamon, cloves and orange and lemon peel, then hot coffee ladled in. A New Orleans tableside ritual credited to Antoine's, and the flavour behind our Café Brûlot Coffee Cake.

entries.title: Soufflé potatoes
entries.summary: Pommes soufflées: thin, even slices of potato fried twice, first in cooler oil to cook them, then in hot oil so they puff into hollow golden pillows. A classic of the old New Orleans houses, often served with béarnaise.

entries.title: Bread pudding soufflé
entries.summary: Commander's Palace's signature: New Orleans bread pudding folded into meringue and baked tall in a ramekin, with whiskey sauce poured into its centre at the table. It marries a set bread custard to a soufflé, and Brennan's does not serve it.

entries.title: Crêpes Suzette at the table
entries.summary: Thin crêpes warmed in beurre Suzette, a sauce of butter, sugar and orange, then flamed with orange liqueur and brandy. A founding flamed dessert whose origin is told in rival stories, still made at the table in the old New Orleans houses.

entries.title: The Brennan's sauce family
entries.say: As it reads: the Brennan's sauce family.
entries.summary: Every sauce on the Brennan's menus placed in the family it comes from: the warm egg emulsions, the brown sauces, the butter sauces, the Creole sauces, the bistro and raw bar sauces, and the sweet sauces of dessert.

entries.title: Eggs Hussarde
entries.summary: The Brennan's signature egg dish: poached eggs on coffee-cured Canadian bacon and housemade English muffins, with marchand de vin, a red wine sauce, beneath and hollandaise on top. New Orleans' answer to Eggs Benedict, under a name older than the restaurant.

entries.title: Eggs Sardou
entries.summary: Poached eggs on artichokes with creamed spinach, a New Orleans classic born at Antoine's and named for the playwright Victorien Sardou. Brennan's sets the eggs on crispy artichokes and Parmesan creamed spinach under Choron, a béarnaise with tomato.

entries.title: Eggs Owen
entries.summary: Short rib débris braised in red wine and pulled, with a Creole-spiced potato and a soft-boiled egg, under the Hussarde's two sauces, hollandaise and marchand de vin. The hearty plate of the Brennan's breakfast and lunch menu: steak and eggs, New Orleans style.

entries.title: The Brennan's Turtle Soup
entries.summary: Brennan's signature soup at breakfast, lunch and dinner: a dark, roux-thickened Creole soup of 100 per cent turtle meat, built on the trinity and a rich stock, finished with aged sherry, brown butter spinach and grated egg.

entries.title: The Brennan's Seafood Gumbo
entries.summary: Brennan's signature gumbo: shrimp, crab and oysters with smoky andouille, simmered into a dark-roux Creole seafood gumbo over Louisiana popcorn rice, served at breakfast, lunch and dinner and as a soup choice on the Traditional Breakfast.

entries.title: Redfish Véronique
entries.summary: The dinner menu's French classic with a Gulf fish: redfish with hibiscus-pickled grapes, braised leeks, fingerling potatoes and a preserved lemon beurre blanc. It is Brennan's take on Sole Véronique and the third course of the dinner tasting.

entries.title: Pecan Gulf Fish
entries.summary: A breakfast and lunch main course: the Gulf fish of the day topped with Louisiana lump crab, with a pecan bordelaise, cauliflower purée and wilted collard greens. Today's fish, which bordelaise, and every nut or shellfish question are settled with the kitchen.

entries.title: The Chateaubriand with Foyot
entries.summary: The thick centre of the beef tenderloin, roasted whole and carved for two, with sauce Foyot, a béarnaise deepened with meat glaze. The cut brings tenderness; the sauce brings the depth the mild meat lacks.

entries.title: The hanger steak with béarnaise
entries.summary: Brennan's breakfast steak and eggs: a Creole-spiced Creekstone Prime hanger, cooked hot and fast, sliced across the grain and served with French béarnaise, a smoked potato pavé and a sunny-side-up egg. The same cut returns at dinner on different foundations.

entries.title: New Orleans Shrimp & Grits
entries.say: As it reads: New Orleans Shrimp & Grits.
entries.summary: Brennan's Creole answer to a Lowcountry breakfast: Louisiana shrimp in a tomato Creole sauce seasoned with tasso, over a fried pimento cheese grit cake, with fried okra chips. Creamy and crisp, smoky and tangy, built on the trinity.

entries.title: Bananas Foster at the table
entries.say: As it reads: Bananas Foster at the table.
entries.summary: Brennan's signature dessert, created in 1951 and flamed at the guéridon: bananas in butter, brown sugar and cinnamon, banana liqueur and burning rum, spooned over housemade vanilla ice cream. The story, the service and the words to say.

entries.title: Breakfast at Brennan's
entries.say: As it reads: Breakfast at Brennan's.
entries.summary: Breakfast at Brennan's is the house's defining idea: a long, celebratory morning meal of an eye opener, a soup, an egg dish and a flamed dessert. Learn its shape, the plates on their foundations and how to sell the morning.

entries.title: Flambé and tableside service
entries.summary: Tableside service brings the last of the cooking into the dining room, on a cart called a guéridon. Learn where it comes from, the flamed desserts it carries at Brennan's, the choreography at the cart and why New Orleans kept it.

entries.title: The menu read by method
entries.say: As it reads: the menu read by method.
entries.summary: The Brennan's menu read by method rather than by dish: steam in a leaf, a blackening pan, the fryer, slow fat, the roasting pan, the rice pot, and the pastry kitchen's custards, caramel and laminated dough. A map from technique to plate.

entries.title: Crème anglaise
entries.summary: Crème anglaise is the French pouring custard: milk, sugar and vanilla cooked gently with egg yolks until it coats a spoon, and never boiled. It is a sauce in its own right and the base of ice cream, Bavarian cream and île flottante.

entries.title: Crème pâtissière
entries.summary: Crème pâtissière, pastry cream, is milk, sugar and egg yolks thickened with flour or cornflour and boiled until it holds its shape. It fills éclairs, tarts and mille-feuille, and is the parent of diplomate, mousseline, chiboust and frangipane.

entries.title: Sabayon
entries.summary: Sabayon is egg yolks, sugar and wine whisked over simmering water into a warm, airy foam. Sweet, it sauces fruit; savoury, made with Champagne or stock, it glazes fish and oysters. The same foam is the first stage of a hollandaise.

entries.title: Pâte à choux
entries.summary: Pâte à choux is a paste of water or milk, butter, flour and eggs, cooked on the stove and baked until steam puffs it hollow. It makes éclairs, profiteroles, Paris-Brest, croquembouche and gougères and, fried, beignets soufflés.

entries.title: Meringues: French, Swiss and Italian
entries.summary: Egg white whipped with sugar into a glossy foam, made three ways: French with raw whites, Swiss warmed over a bain-marie, a bowl set over simmering water, and Italian with hot syrup. Each has its strengths and faults, and all three need a clean bowl.

entries.title: Caramel and the sugar stages
entries.summary: Sugar boiled through its named stages, from thread to hard crack and into caramel, read by thermometer and by colour. It can be made dry or wet, is stopped with warm cream and runs through Brennan's desserts, from the Foster to the bread pudding.

entries.title: Bananas Foster
entries.summary: Bananas turned in a caramel of butter, brown sugar and cinnamon, loosened with banana liqueur, flamed with dark rum and spooned warm over vanilla ice cream. The fruit must be ripe but firm and the caramel smooth and blond before the rum is lit.

entries.title: New Orleans bread pudding
entries.say: As it reads: New Orleans bread pudding.
entries.summary: Stale French bread soaked in a sweet, spiced custard and baked until just set, served warm with a whiskey sauce. A thrift dish New Orleans made its own, because the city's light bread drinks custard without turning to paste.

entries.title: Pain perdu
entries.summary: Pain perdu, lost bread, is stale bread soaked in a sweet custard of egg, milk, sugar and spice, then fried in butter until golden outside and just set within. It is the Creole name for French toast, and an old New Orleans breakfast.

entries.title: Beignets
entries.summary: New Orleans beignets are squares of rich yeast dough fried until they puff hollow, then buried in icing sugar and eaten hot. Café du Monde, a French Market coffee stand since 1862, serves them with café au lait, and visitors often ask about them.

entries.title: Pralines
entries.summary: New Orleans pralines are pecan sweets of white and brown sugar, butter and cream, cooked to the soft ball, beaten until creamy and spooned into rounds that set soft like fudge. They descend from a French sugared almond, remade by the city's Creole cooks.

entries.title: Bavarian cream
entries.say: As it reads: Bavarian cream, or bavarois, bah-vahr-WAH.
entries.summary: Bavarian cream, bavarois in French, is crème anglaise set with gelatine and lightened with whipped cream, then chilled in a mould and turned out. Silky and light yet able to stand, it sits between a mousse and a custard.

entries.title: The brigade de cuisine
entries.summary: The brigade de cuisine is the kitchen's chain of command, from the chef de cuisine down to the commis and the plongeur. It tells every cook what they own, who they answer to and how a whole kitchen moves as one.

entries.title: The stations
entries.summary: A station, or partie, is one part of the kitchen with one job: sauces, fish, roasts, grill, fryer, vegetables, cold food, pastry. Knowing which station cooks what tells a cook where to stand and a server why a plate may be running late.

entries.title: Calls on the line
entries.say: As it reads: calls on the line.
entries.summary: Calls are the short spoken words a kitchen runs on: oui chef, heard, behind, hot, fire, all day, eighty-six. Each says one thing fast and each is answered, so orders are heard and bodies and blades stay out of harm.

entries.title: The pass and expediting
entries.say: As it reads: the pass and expediting.
entries.summary: The pass is the counter between kitchen and dining room where every plate is checked before it goes. The expediter runs it, reading tickets, firing courses and timing each table so its plates leave together, hot and right.

entries.title: Menu French a server says
entries.summary: The few dozen French words an American menu still carries: the little joining words, the course names, the ways a meal is priced, and the sauce and cooking words guests ask about. Say each simply, then in plain English.

entries.title: Mise en place words
entries.summary: The French names a classical kitchen uses for its pans, strainers, herb bundles, prep jobs and flavour bases. Read at sight, they turn a prep list into clear work: monder the tomatoes, a bouquet garni for the stock, duxelles for the filling.

entries.title: The cuts by name
entries.say: As it reads: the cuts by name.
entries.summary: The French names for the classical cuts: strips, dice, slices and shapes, from julienne to tourné, and the garnish names that promise a cut. Each name is a promise of shape, on a prep list and on a menu.

entries.title: Cooking terms on the ticket
entries.say: As it reads: cooking terms on the ticket.
entries.summary: The words that carry an order from the table to the kitchen: doneness in French and English, egg orders, modifiers such as no, add, sub and on the side, seat numbers, and an allergy written down and said to the kitchen.

entries.title: The old French dish names
entries.say: As it reads: the old French dish names.
entries.summary: Classical French cooking names dishes for garnishes, regions and people, and each name promises what is on the plate: Clamart means peas, Argenteuil asparagus, Rossini foie gras and truffle. New Orleans added names of its own.

entries.title: Say it: the Brennan's menu
entries.say: As it reads: say it, the Brennan's menu.
entries.summary: The house's say-it list: the French and Louisiana words a server says most on the Brennan's menu, each with the house guide's respelling, from hollandaise and Hussarde to roux and pralines, and the habit of saying each name, then what it is.

entries.title: La Varenne
entries.summary: François Pierre de La Varenne, cook to the Marquis d'Uxelles, published Le Cuisinier françois in 1651. It traded heavy spice for the taste of the food itself and set down bouillon, roux and reduction as working tools.

entries.title: Carême
entries.summary: Marie-Antoine Carême (1784 to 1833), the Paris pastry cook who rose to cook for Talleyrand, the Prince Regent, Tsar Alexander I and the Rothschilds. He built sugar architecture, sorted sauces into four great families and set grand cooking down in books.

entries.title: Escoffier
entries.summary: Georges Auguste Escoffier (1846 to 1935) ran the kitchens of César Ritz's hotels, organised the kitchen into stations and set the classical repertoire down in Le Guide culinaire of 1903, simplifying Carême's grand style for the restaurant.

entries.title: The roots of Creole cooking
entries.say: As it reads: the roots of Creole cooking.
entries.summary: Creole cooking is the cooking of New Orleans: French at its base and built by many hands, Spanish rulers, West African and Caribbean cooks, Native American neighbours, German and Italian settlers. The Acadians gave rise to its country cousin, Cajun.

entries.title: Lafcadio Hearn's La Cuisine Créole
entries.summary: La Cuisine Créole, printed in 1885 and generally credited to Lafcadio Hearn, is among the first books of Creole cooking: a record of gumbos, courtbouillon, jambalaya and sauces as New Orleans cooked them while a world's fair filled the city.

entries.title: The Picayune's Creole Cook Book
entries.summary: The Picayune's Creole Cook Book, published by the Daily Picayune around 1900, set down the cooking of the city's Black Creole cooks. Reprinted for decades, it is a source for dishes and words, not a set of exact modern recipes.

entries.title: Antoine's
entries.summary: Antoine's, founded in 1840 by Antoine Alciatore of Marseille, calls itself the oldest family-run restaurant in the United States. It is credited with Oysters Rockefeller, café brûlot and Eggs Sardou, and a novel about it inspired Breakfast at Brennan's.

entries.title: Galatoire's
entries.summary: Galatoire's, opened on Bourbon Street in 1905 by Jean Galatoire, is the French Quarter house known for its customs: a line on the pavement for the downstairs room, the long Friday lunch, jackets in the evening and waiters kept for decades.

entries.title: Arnaud's
entries.summary: Arnaud's, opened in 1918 by Arnaud Cazenave, a French wine salesman known as Count Arnaud, is one of the grand old French Creole houses of the French Quarter: Shrimp Arnaud, soufflé potatoes, flaming café brûlot and the French 75 Bar.

entries.title: Commander's Palace
entries.summary: Commander's Palace is the Garden District restaurant Emile Commander opened in the late nineteenth century, owned by members of the Brennan family since around 1970. Its kitchen was led by Paul Prudhomme and Emeril Lagasse, and it is a separate business from Brennan's.

entries.title: Owen and Ella Brennan
entries.say: As it reads: Owen and Ella Brennan.
entries.summary: Owen Brennan opened the restaurant on Bourbon Street in 1946; his younger sister Ella carried it to 417 Royal Street after his death and later led Commander's Palace. Their story, told briefly and accurately, sits behind every signature plate.

entries.title: Paul Blangé
entries.summary: Paul Blangé, the Dutch-born first chef of Brennan's, led its kitchen from 1946 into the 1970s and created Bananas Foster in 1951, at Owen Brennan's request. His story teaches how to credit a dish: created here, credited with, or made famous here.

entries.title: Paul Prudhomme
entries.summary: Paul Prudhomme (1940 to 2015), a Cajun farm boy from near Opelousas, ran the kitchen at Commander's Palace from 1975, opened K-Paul's in 1979, created blackened redfish and taught the country to cook Louisiana food.

entries.title: Leah Chase
entries.summary: Leah Chase (1923 to 2019), the Queen of Creole Cuisine, cooked for some seven decades at Dooky Chase's in Tremé, feeding civil rights leaders, presidents and her neighbours, and showed that Creole cooking is a Black Creole tradition.

entries.title: Holding hollandaise and warm emulsions
entries.say: As it reads: holding hollandaise, HOL-un-dayz, and warm emulsions.
entries.summary: How a kitchen keeps hollandaise, béarnaise and beurre blanc warm enough to stay smooth and cool enough not to scramble or split, and the written time limit, labels and clean containers that keep a warm egg and butter sauce fit to serve.

entries.title: Eggs and safety
entries.say: As it reads: eggs and safety.
entries.summary: Why a runny yolk or a raw-egg sauce carries a risk of Salmonella, who it matters to most, and the habits that manage it: cold storage, clean hands, pasteurised eggs where the kitchen chooses them, and the menu's consumer advisory.

entries.title: Raw and cooked oysters
entries.say: As it reads: raw and cooked oysters.
entries.summary: Why a raw Gulf oyster carries a rare but serious risk from Vibrio vulnificus, who it matters to most, the warnings Louisiana and the menu require, the shellstock tags, and how cooking and cold, careful handling change the picture.

entries.title: Cooling stocks and sauces
entries.say: As it reads: cooling stocks and sauces.
entries.summary: Cooked food that will be kept must lose its heat quickly, in two timed stages, so the bacteria that survive cooking never get the warm hours they need. Big, thick pots need the most help.

entries.title: The danger zone and hot holding
entries.say: As it reads: the danger zone and hot holding.
entries.summary: The danger zone is 5 to 57°C (41 to 135°F), where bacteria multiply fastest. Food is held above or below it, checked with a calibrated thermometer, or kept on a written clock and served or thrown away by its marked time.

entries.title: Cooking temperatures and the consumer advisory
entries.say: As it reads: cooking temperatures and the consumer advisory.
entries.summary: The Food Code sets a minimum internal temperature and time for each raw animal food. Learn the figures, probe the thickest part, and know why a seared whole steak may be served rare, and why tartare and rosy duck call for the consumer advisory.

entries.title: Shellfish handling
entries.summary: How a kitchen keeps crab, crawfish and shrimp fit to serve: live ones cool, damp and lively, picked meat and tails cold, frozen shrimp thawed the right way, raw kept apart from cooked, and the allergen carried in shells, stock and fryer oil.

entries.title: Flambé safety at the table
entries.say: As it reads: flambé, flahm-BAY, safety at the table.
entries.summary: The habits that keep a flame at the table a show and never a fire: the spirit measured first, the pan off the flame when it goes in, clear space around the cart, a lid in reach and the burner off before leaving.

entries.title: Cross-contact and the allergen conversation
entries.say: As it reads: cross-contact and the allergen conversation.
entries.summary: What every server and cook must know: the nine major food allergens the law names, how cross-contact carries them onto a plate that never listed them, where they hide on a Creole menu, and the routine that takes every question to the kitchen.

careme.note: Carême, early in the nineteenth century, sorted the French sauces into families under four great sauces: espagnole, velouté, allemande and béchamel. Allemande is now taught as a daughter of velouté. Escoffier's Le Guide culinaire (1903) named four base sauces, espagnole, velouté, béchamel and tomate; the 1907 English translation printed hollandaise among its leading warm sauces, and later teaching made five the mothers taught today.

rungs.name: White roux
rungs.cue: As pale as the flour, bubbling gently into a smooth paste like wet sand, with no colour at all
rungs.smell: The raw, pasty smell of flour gives way to cooked pastry or plain biscuit
rungs.thickening: The strongest on the ladder: the starch is barely changed, so a little roux thickens a lot of milk

rungs.name: Blond roux
rungs.cue: Pale straw to light gold, the colour of sand, a little looser in the pan
rungs.smell: Toasted bread with a hint of popcorn, and no raw flour left
rungs.thickening: Nearly as strong as white: the starch is only lightly toasted, so it still binds stock into a coating sauce

rungs.name: Peanut butter roux
rungs.cue: Light tan, the colour of smooth peanut butter, running more freely off the spoon
rungs.smell: Roasted peanuts, deeper and nuttier than toast
rungs.thickening: Noticeably weaker than blond, yet still enough body for a thick, smothered sauce

rungs.name: Milk chocolate roux (medium brown)
rungs.cue: Medium brown, the colour of milk chocolate or a hazelnut shell, loose and glossy in the pot
rungs.smell: Toasted nuts turning towards cocoa, roasted and deep
rungs.thickening: Much weaker: from here a roux gives more flavour than body, so recipes call for more of it

rungs.name: Dark chocolate roux (brick)
rungs.cue: Deep red brown, the colour of dark chocolate or old brick, thin and shiny; black flecks mean it has burnt
rungs.smell: Deep roast, close to coffee and cocoa; a sharp, acrid smell means it has gone too far
rungs.thickening: The weakest: a dark roux mostly colours and flavours, so even a thin gumbo takes a generous amount
